objectives.text: Define and describe fundamental pharmacologic concepts, including pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, drug-receptor interactions, dose-response relationships, therapeutic index, half-life, and steady state.
Describe the processes of drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion and factors that influence these processes.
Explain how patient-specific factors, including age, pregnancy, renal and hepatic function, and pharmacogenetic variation, may affect medication response.
objectives.thin_note: Age and pregnancy are only named in the prescribing checklist

objectives.text: Identify common types and mechanisms of adverse drug reactions, drug-drug interactions, and drug-disease interactions.
Interpret common components of medication orders and prescriptions, including drug name, dose, route, frequency, and duration.
objectives.thin_note: Only dose, route, interval, and monitoring (checklist, renal dosing); no prescription-reading content

objectives.text: Explain drug biotransformation (Phase I/II metabolism) and the clinical impact of CYP450 enzyme inhibition and induction.
Explain mechanisms of drug excretion and how renal function affects dosing.
Calculate and apply basic pharmacokinetic parameters (half-life, steady state, clearance).
Describe how pharmacogenomic variation can alter drug response.
Apply a structured framework to clinical prescribing decisions.

about.text: Session 2 of 2 on Introduction to Pharmacology (Thursday, October 22): metabolism, excretion, PK calculations, pharmacogenomics & clinical integration.

Recap: Session 1 covered pharmacology vocabulary, drug development, pharmacodynamics, dose-response relationships, and ADME through distribution. Today picks up with metabolism (Section 6) and runs through the integrated clinical framework and recall quiz.

The Lecture Recall Quiz is a cumulative self-test covering both sessions — a standalone recall resource, separate from the in-lecture quick checks; revisit it on your own before the exam. (Rebuilt here as practice questions.)

**Original figures in this deck:** Figures 6–8 (CYP450 inhibition vs. induction; exponential decay over half-lives; reaching steady state with and without a loading dose) were generated by the course director using the AI tool Claude to illustrate standard, non-copyrighted pharmacologic concepts — original diagrams, not reproduced from Katzung or any other copyrighted source. **Reference:** Anthropic. definitions.text: Drug metabolism = how the body chemically transforms drugs.
Phase I — Functionalization: oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis.
Phase II — Conjugation: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, methylation, glutathione conjugation.
**Enzyme inhibition:** a drug slows a CYP enzyme, raising the blood level of any drug that CYP normally clears.
**Enzyme induction:** a drug increases CYP enzyme production, lowering the blood level (and effect) of drugs that CYP clears.
**Microsomal mixed-function oxidase system:** the Phase I machinery in the smooth endoplasmic reticulum; needs cytochrome P450, NADPH-P450 reductase, NADPH and molecular oxygen.
**Cytochrome P450** is named for the 450-nm light absorption of its carbon-monoxide complex. It has very low substrate specificity: high lipid solubility is the one thing its substrates share.

how.text: Why metabolize? To inactivate an active drug, making it easier to excrete.
To activate a prodrug into its active form.
To produce an active metabolite that contributes to (or extends) the drug effect.
**Occasionally to produce a toxic metabolite — the basis of some drug-induced organ injury.**
Phase I is primarily carried out by cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes and often creates or unmasks a reactive functional group.
Phase II attaches a polar group to the molecule, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion.
Phase I often comes before Phase II, but not always — some drugs go straight to conjugation.
Inhibition slows clearance (substrate level rises); induction speeds clearance (substrate level falls).
CYP3A4 alone metabolizes over 50% of the prescription drugs metabolized by the liver.

Acetaminophen is mostly conjugated (glucuronide/sulfate); in overdose glutathione is depleted and the toxic metabolite (NAPQI) injures the liver — **N-acetylcysteine** given within 8–16 hours protects against fulminant hepatotoxicity.
Share of liver P450: CYP3A4 about 30%, CYP2C9 about 20%, CYP1A2 about 15%, CYP2E1 about 10%, CYP2D6 about 5%. CYP3A4 handles over 50% of liver-metabolized prescription drugs.

Inducers act through receptors that switch on CYP genes: **AhR** (tobacco smoke, charcoal-broiled meat, cruciferous vegetables, omeprazole → CYP1A) and **PXR** (rifampin, St. John’s wort, dexamethasone, phenobarbital → CYP3A).

**Commensal gut microbiota** metabolize drugs too: they reduce digoxin, so antibiotics such as erythromycin or tetracycline can double digoxin levels; bacterial β-glucuronidases free glucuronidated drugs for reabsorption (enterohepatic recycling).
An inducer can speed up its own metabolism, producing **pharmacokinetic tolerance**: the same dose works less over time.

clinical.text: CYP450 interactions are one of the highest-yield concepts in all of pharmacology — nearly every major drug class has at least one clinically important CYP interaction.
**Example: Drug A inhibits CYP3A4 → Drug B (a CYP3A4 substrate) accumulates → toxicity risk rises.**
Inhibition pushes a substrate's level ABOVE 100% of baseline (toxicity risk); induction pushes it BELOW 100% (therapeutic-failure risk).
Inhibiting the CYP that clears a substrate is especially dangerous when the substrate has a narrow therapeutic index.
Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition.
Liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis, hepatitis) slows metabolism of some drugs enough that ordinary doses can cause coma.
Severe ADRs contribute to about 100,000 US deaths a year and about 7% of hospital admissions.
Smoking induces CYP1A enzymes and can change the metabolism of other drugs.

**Diet and environmental factors** change drug metabolism: charcoal-broiled food and cruciferous vegetables induce CYP1A, grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A, smokers and pesticide-exposed workers clear some drugs faster, which complicates dosing of narrow-TI drugs.
Stopping an inducer is as risky as starting one: when a sedative inducer is stopped, warfarin metabolism slows, levels rise and bleeding can follow.
Pharmacogenomic testing is still rarely used, although severe ADRs cause about 100,000 US deaths a year and about 7% of hospital admissions.

examples.text: NAPQI (from acetaminophen) is the textbook example of a toxic metabolite produced by normal Phase I metabolism — previewing the acetaminophen toxicity lecture.
CYP3A4 — the enzyme in the lecture's inhibitor/substrate example.
**Inducers:** rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, barbiturates, St. John's wort; **inhibitors:** ketoconazole, clarithromycin/erythromycin, ritonavir, grapefruit juice.
St. John's wort induces CYP3A4 and speeds metabolism of oral contraceptives, warfarin, cyclosporine, and others.
CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, grapefruit juice) with terfenadine caused fatal torsades de pointes, and terfenadine was withdrawn.
Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, so the mercaptopurine dose must be reduced when both are given.

traps.text: Inhibitor → substrate level UP (toxicity); inducer → substrate level DOWN (therapeutic failure). Don't swap them.
CYP3A4 is a Phase I (CYP450) enzyme — it does not "only affect Phase II metabolism."
Not every drug goes through Phase I first — some go straight to Phase II conjugation.

hooks.text: Why does an inhibitor cause toxicity? The CYP enzyme that normally clears the substrate is slowed, so the substrate can no longer be cleared normally and accumulates.
Why does Phase II help excretion? Attaching a polar group makes the drug more water-soluble, so it can leave in urine or bile.
**IN**hibitor = level goes **IN**to the danger zone (↑, toxicity). In**DU**cer = level goes **D**own (↓, failure).
Phase **I** = **I**nitial change (oxidize, reduce, hydrolyze — CYP450). Phase **II** = **T**ag it (conjugate a polar group → water-soluble).

high_yield.text: Phase I (CYP450): oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis. Phase II: conjugation → water-soluble.
Narrow-TI substrate + CYP inhibitor = especially dangerous.
Metabolism can produce toxic metabolites (e.g., NAPQI).

questions.stem: In Figure 6, the "+ Enzyme inhibitor" bar rises to 240% of baseline, while the "+ Enzyme inducer" bar falls to 42%. For a patient on a stable dose of the substrate drug, which condition poses the greatest risk of toxicity?
questions.correct: Enzyme inhibition, because it raises the substrate drug's blood level
questions.why_correct: The inhibitor bar at 240% shows the substrate accumulating because it can no longer be cleared normally, raising toxicity risk (S9).

distractors.text: Enzyme induction, because it lowers the substrate drug's blood level
distractors.why: The inducer bar (42%) shows the opposite problem — therapeutic failure, not toxicity (S9).

distractors.text: Normal metabolism, because the substrate is cleared at baseline
distractors.why: Baseline (100%) is the reference level, not the highest-risk state (S7-9).

distractors.text: Neither condition, because CYP changes do not alter drug levels
distractors.why: Both conditions clearly change the substrate's level (S7).

distractors.text: Both equally, because any CYP change doubles the toxicity risk
distractors.why: Only inhibition raises the level; induction lowers it (S6, S9).

questions.stem: A patient stable on a CYP3A4-substrate medication with a narrow therapeutic index is started on a new drug that is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the most likely consequence?
questions.correct: Increased substrate drug level and increased toxicity risk
questions.why_correct: Inhibiting the CYP enzyme that clears the substrate slows its metabolism and raises its level — especially dangerous with a narrow therapeutic index (S11).

distractors.text: No change, since CYP3A4 only affects Phase II metabolism
distractors.why: CYP450 enzymes carry out Phase I metabolism (S5).

distractors.text: Decreased substrate drug level and reduced drug effect
distractors.why: That is the effect of an INDUCER, not an inhibitor (S6).

distractors.text: Increased renal clearance of the substrate drug overall
distractors.why: A CYP inhibitor slows metabolic clearance; it doesn't raise renal clearance (S6, S11).

distractors.text: Decreased substrate level from faster CYP3A4 clearance
distractors.why: Faster clearance describes induction; an inhibitor slows clearance (S6).

questions.stem: Drug A, a CYP enzyme inducer, is started in a patient taking Drug B, a substrate of that same CYP enzyme. What happens to Drug B's level and effect?
questions.correct: Decreases, risking therapeutic failure
questions.why_correct: Enzyme induction speeds substrate clearance, lowering its level and effect — the opposite of inhibition (S48).

distractors.text: Increases, raising toxicity risk
distractors.why: Rising levels and toxicity follow an INHIBITOR (S6).

distractors.text: No change in level or effect
distractors.why: Induction lowers the level and effect of drugs that CYP clears (S6).

distractors.text: Elimination changes to biliary
distractors.why: Induction changes how fast the drug is cleared, not its route (S48).

distractors.text: Increases, then quickly normalizes
distractors.why: Induction lowers, not raises, the substrate level (S6, S48).

questions.stem: A drug undergoes glucuronidation, which attaches a polar group to the molecule. Which statement best describes this step?
questions.correct: A Phase II conjugation that makes the drug more water-soluble for excretion
questions.why_correct: Glucuronidation is a Phase II (conjugation) reaction that attaches a polar group, producing a more water-soluble product for renal/biliary excretion (S5).

distractors.text: A Phase I oxidation that unmasks a reactive functional group on the drug
distractors.why: Oxidation is Phase I; glucuronidation is Phase II conjugation (S5).

distractors.text: A CYP450-driven hydrolysis that always precedes any Phase II reaction
distractors.why: Hydrolysis is Phase I, and Phase I does not always come first (S5, S5 notes).

distractors.text: A Phase II reaction that makes the drug more lipophilic and longer-acting
distractors.why: Phase II produces a more water-soluble (polar) product (S5).

distractors.text: A reduction reaction that converts a prodrug into its active form
distractors.why: Reduction is a Phase I reaction (S5).

questions.stem: A 19-year-old arrives 6 hours after a large intentional acetaminophen ingestion. Labs are pending. Which treatment best protects against fulminant liver injury?
questions.correct: N-acetylcysteine, started within the 8–16 hour window
questions.why_correct: N-acetylcysteine given within 8–16 hours protects against acetaminophen hepatotoxicity by replacing depleted glutathione (p. 66).

distractors.text: Sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine and speed excretion
distractors.why: Urine alkalinization is used for aspirin overdose, a weak acid (p. 20).

distractors.text: Rifampin to induce CYP enzymes and clear the drug faster
distractors.why: Induction would increase toxic metabolite formation, not protect the liver (p. 66).

distractors.text: Protamine to bind and neutralize the circulating drug
distractors.why: Protamine neutralizes heparin (p. 26), not acetaminophen.

distractors.text: Waiting for levels before giving any treatment at all
distractors.why: The protective window is 8–16 hours, so delay risks liver failure (p. 66).

questions.stem: A heavy smoker on a CYP1A2-metabolized drug quits smoking abruptly. What should the PA anticipate?
questions.correct: Drug levels may rise as CYP1A induction fades
questions.why_correct: Tobacco smoke induces CYP1A through AhR; when the inducer stops, metabolism slows and levels can rise (p. 60; p. 72).

distractors.text: Drug levels will fall because metabolism speeds up
distractors.why: Quitting removes induction, so metabolism slows (p. 60).

distractors.text: No change, since smoking affects only the lungs
distractors.why: Smoke chemicals induce liver CYP1A enzymes (p. 60).

distractors.text: Renal clearance will double right away
distractors.why: The effect is on hepatic metabolism, not renal clearance (p. 60).

distractors.text: The drug becomes a prodrug that needs activation
distractors.why: Quitting does not change how the drug is activated (p. 60).

steps: Drug B (CYP3A4 substrate) cleared more slowly

steps: Small fraction → CYP → NAPQI, detoxified by glutathione
Overdose: glutathione depleted → NAPQI injures the liver

definitions.text: Drug excretion = clearing drug from the body.
**Glomerular filtration:** free (unbound) drug passes from blood into the renal tubule based on molecular size.
**Tubular secretion:** active transporters move additional drug from blood into the tubule.
**Tubular reabsorption:** lipophilic, un-ionized drug can passively diffuse back into the blood, reducing net elimination.

how.text: Kidney: the dominant route for most drugs and metabolites.
Bile / feces: important for some large or protein-bound drugs.
Lungs: volatile agents (e.g., anesthetic gases).
Sweat / breast milk: minor routes, but breast milk matters for lactating patients.
**Decreased renal function → decreased drug clearance → increased drug exposure and accumulation risk.**

clinical.text: eGFR and creatinine clearance (CrCl) are the standard bedside estimates of renal function used to adjust dosing.
Any renally-cleared, narrow-therapeutic-index drug (think: many antibiotics, digoxin, lithium) needs a dose or interval adjustment in renal impairment.
For a primarily renally eliminated drug when eGFR drops: decrease the dose and/or extend the dosing interval, guided by eGFR/CrCl.
Urine pH manipulation (e.g., alkalinizing urine in aspirin overdose) works by trapping ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption.
This is the PK foundation for the renal-impairment case and the NSAID-in-CKD case later.

examples.text: Renally-cleared, narrow-TI drugs: many antibiotics, digoxin, lithium.
Aspirin overdose — urine alkalinization traps ionized drug.
Anesthetic gases — eliminated by the lungs.

traps.text: Only FREE (unbound) drug is filtered at the glomerulus.
Reabsorption REDUCES net elimination — and only lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed.
Renal impairment → lower dose and/or longer interval — NOT "no adjustment," a higher dose, or "IV only."

comparisons.title: Routes of drug elimination
rows: Breast milk matters for lactating patients

hooks.text: Why does alkalinizing urine help in aspirin overdose? It keeps the drug ionized in the tubule, and only un-ionized drug can diffuse back — so reabsorption is blocked and more drug leaves.
Why adjust doses in CKD? Less renal function → less clearance → more exposure and accumulation of renally-cleared drugs.
Kidney handling = "**F**ilter, **S**ecrete, **R**eabsorb" — **F**ree drug filtered, **S**ecreted by transporters, **R**eabsorbed if lipophilic & un-ionized.

high_yield.text: Kidney = dominant elimination route; filtration (free drug), secretion (transporters), reabsorption (lipophilic, un-ionized).
**↓ renal function → ↓ clearance → ↑ exposure** → lower dose and/or longer interval, guided by **eGFR/CrCl**.
Renally cleared narrow-TI drugs: many antibiotics, digoxin, lithium.

questions.stem: A patient's eGFR drops significantly due to new chronic kidney disease. For a drug that is primarily renally eliminated, what dosing adjustment is most appropriate?
questions.correct: Decrease the dose and/or extend the dosing interval
questions.why_correct: Reduced renal clearance raises exposure to renally-eliminated drugs; the standard response is a lower dose, a longer interval, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl (S17).

distractors.text: No dose or interval adjustment is needed
distractors.why: Decreased renal function raises exposure and accumulation risk (S15).

distractors.text: Increase the dose to maintain the effect
distractors.why: Exposure is already increased; a higher dose would worsen accumulation (S15).

distractors.text: Switch to IV administration only for now
distractors.why: Route doesn't fix reduced renal clearance; adjust dose/interval (S17).

distractors.text: Shorten the dosing interval to every few hours
distractors.why: Intervals should be EXTENDED, not shortened, in renal impairment (S17).

questions.stem: A patient arrives after an aspirin overdose, and the team alkalinizes the urine. How does this increase elimination of the drug?
questions.correct: It traps ionized drug in the tubule, blocking its reabsorption
questions.why_correct: Urine pH manipulation works by trapping ionized drug in the tubule, blocking reabsorption (S14 notes); only lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed (S14).

distractors.text: It increases glomerular filtration of protein-bound drug
distractors.why: Only free (unbound) drug is filtered (S14).

distractors.text: It activates tubular transporters that secrete the drug
distractors.why: Secretion uses active transporters (S14), but urine pH works by blocking reabsorption (S14 notes).

distractors.text: It makes the drug more lipophilic so it is reabsorbed
distractors.why: Lipophilic, un-ionized drug is reabsorbed — the opposite of the goal (S14).

distractors.text: It shifts elimination from the kidney to bile and feces
distractors.why: The mechanism acts in the renal tubule (S14 notes).

questions.stem: Which renal process REDUCES the net elimination of a drug?
questions.correct: Passive reabsorption of lipophilic, un-ionized drug
questions.why_correct: Tubular reabsorption: lipophilic, un-ionized drug passively diffuses back into the blood, reducing net elimination (S14).

distractors.text: Glomerular filtration of free, unbound drug
distractors.why: Filtration moves drug INTO the tubule (S14).

distractors.text: Tubular secretion by active transporters
distractors.why: Secretion moves additional drug INTO the tubule (S14).

distractors.text: Filtration of drug based on molecular size
distractors.why: This is glomerular filtration, which adds drug to the tubule (S14).

distractors.text: Excretion of volatile agents by the lungs
distractors.why: Lung elimination removes volatile agents; it's not a renal process (S13).

classes.name: PK Calculations: Half-Life, Steady State & Clearance

definitions.text: **Half-life (t½) = the time required for the plasma drug concentration to fall by 50%.**
**Steady state:** the point at which drug intake equals drug elimination; reached in about 4–5 half-lives with regular dosing.
**Loading dose:** a larger initial dose used to rapidly reach a therapeutic concentration, without waiting for steady state.
**Maintenance dose:** the regular, ongoing dose that keeps the drug within the therapeutic range once steady state is reached.
**Clearance = the volume of plasma from which drug is completely removed per unit time.**
**t½ = 0.7 × Vd / CL** — half-life rises when Vd rises or clearance falls.
**Loading dose = Vd × target concentration** (e.g., theophylline: 35 L × 10 mg/L = 350 mg for a 70-kg adult).

**Extraction ratio (ER):** hepatic clearance divided by hepatic blood flow (about 90 L/h). Oral bioavailability ≈ fraction absorbed × (1 − ER); morphine’s ER of 0.67 predicts about 33% oral bioavailability.

**Target concentration approach** (the rational way to design a dosage regimen): pick the concentration that gives the desired effect, then individualize the dose from the patient’s clearance and volume of distribution.

**Zero-order absorption** runs at a constant rate (gastric emptying, controlled-release forms); **first-order** absorption is proportional to the amount left, nearly complete after four absorption half-lives.

how.text: PK calculations = the math PAs actually use at the bedside.
Half-life is determined by clearance and volume of distribution together — it is not a fixed drug "property" independent of physiology.
A drug is roughly 97% eliminated after about 5 half-lives.
**Formula: % remaining = 100% x (1/2)^(number of half-life)** — i.e., per number of half-lives elapsed.
**Formula: C(t) = C₀ x (1/2)^(t/t½)** — C₀ = starting concentration, t = time elapsed.
Worked example (both formulas): t½ = 6 h; an IV dose gives a starting plasma concentration of 100 mg/L — see the table for each half-life.
Clearance determines how efficiently a drug is removed — and, along with Vd, determines half-life.
Total clearance is usually the sum of hepatic and renal clearance.
Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance.
Steady state takes ~4–5 half-lives regardless of dose size — the same reason a drug is ~97% eliminated ~5 half-lives after stopping it.
Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life.
During regular dosing: 50% of steady state after 1 half-life, 75% after 2, and over 90% after 4 — the textbook's "four half-lives" rule of thumb.
If the dosing interval is shorter than four half-lives, accumulation will be detectable.
**Capacity-limited (saturable) elimination:** clearance falls as concentration rises — important for phenytoin, ethanol, and aspirin.

**Maintenance dosing rate = clearance × target concentration** (divide by F for oral). The average steady-state level depends only on clearance; the dosing interval changes only the peaks and troughs.

Effects do not always follow plasma levels: enalapril (half-life about 4 hours) still works once daily because its peak is far above its C₅₀; delays come from distribution, slow receptor release (digoxin) or slow turnover of a body substance (warfarin and clotting factors).
Half-life can change without clearance changing: diazepam’s half-life lengthens with age because its volume of distribution grows, not because metabolism slows.

clinical.text: Case: significant CKD + a medication primarily eliminated unchanged by the kidney. **What happens to the drug's concentration and half-life, and would you adjust the dose, the dosing interval, or both?**

**Clinical pearl:** reduced clearance raises drug concentration and prolongs half-life; many renally-cleared drugs are managed by extending the dosing interval, reducing the dose, or both, guided by eGFR/CrCl.
The logic chain: clearance ↓ → half-life ↑ → time to steady state ↑ → accumulation risk ↑ if the regimen is not adjusted.
Reduced renal clearance raises both drug concentration and half-life.
A loading dose reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives; it does not change the maintenance dose or remove the need for monitoring.

Highly extracted drugs (morphine, isoniazid, propranolol, lidocaine, verapamil) vary widely in bioavailability between patients, and much more drug gets through in cirrhosis with portosystemic shunting. Lidocaine is never given orally because of toxic metabolites.

**Schedule-dependent effects:** the same average level can carry different toxicity; gentamicin is more nephrotoxic as a constant infusion than as intermittent doses, because high peaks saturate its uptake into the renal cortex.
Give IV loading doses slowly (over an hour, not seconds): a fast bolus can overshoot into toxicity before the drug distributes, e.g., phenytoin.
Timing drug levels: digoxin at least 6 hours after the dose, lithium just before the next dose; for steady-state estimates sample mid-interval after at least three half-lives.
In obesity, dose drugs that stay out of fat (gentamicin, digoxin) on fat-free mass; edema and ascites enlarge gentamicin’s volume of distribution.
Changes in plasma protein binding rarely matter clinically: the body simply eliminates the extra unbound drug.

examples.text: Not covered in materials — this section uses illustrative drugs ("a drug with a half-life of 6 hours").
Theophylline worked example: clearance 2.8 L/h × target 10 mg/L = 28 mg/h IV; loading dose = 35 L × 10 mg/L = 350 mg.

traps.text: After 3 half-lives, 12.5% REMAINS (87.5% eliminated) — read whether the question asks remaining or eliminated.
Time to steady state depends on half-life — not on dose size, bioavailability, or route.
Half-life is not a fixed property — it changes with clearance and Vd (e.g., in renal impairment).
A loading dose does NOT permanently lower the maintenance dose or eliminate monitoring.

figures.title: Textbook concept · Five to fill, five to empty
figures.caption: Original diagram: starting regular dosing, each half-life closes half of the remaining gap to steady state (50 → 75 → 87.5 → 93.75 → ~97%); after stopping, each half-life removes half of what remains (50 → 25 → 12.5 → 6.25 → 3.125%). The same 4–5 half-lives govern both.

hooks.text: Why does CKD prolong half-life? Half-life depends on clearance (with Vd) — less renal clearance means the concentration takes longer to fall by 50%, so the drug accumulates.
Why does a loading dose skip the wait? It is a larger first dose that reaches the therapeutic concentration right away instead of building up over ~4–5 half-lives.
"**Five to fill, five to empty**": ~4–5 half-lives to reach steady state; ~5 half-lives to be ~97% eliminated.

high_yield.text: **t½** = time for plasma concentration to fall 50%; set by **clearance + Vd**.
Each t½ halves what remains: 50 → 25 → 12.5 → 6.25 → ~3% (~97% eliminated at 5 t½).
**Steady state ≈ 4–5 t½**, regardless of dose; loading dose gets there immediately.
**Clearance** = plasma volume cleared per unit time; total = hepatic + renal.
CKD: clearance ↓ → t½ ↑ → concentration ↑ → adjust dose and/or interval.

questions.stem: Using Figure 7, approximately what percentage of the original drug concentration remains after 3 half-lives (3 t½)?
questions.why_correct: Each half-life halves what remains: 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% after 3 t½ (S22).

distractors.why: 50% remains after 1 half-life (S22).
25% remains after 2 half-lives (S22).
About 3% remains after 5 half-lives (S22).
6.25% remains after 4 half-lives (S19).

questions.stem: In Figure 8, the dashed loading-dose line starts at the target concentration immediately, while the maintenance-only line climbs gradually over several doses. What is the clinical advantage of adding a loading dose?
questions.correct: It reaches the therapeutic target immediately instead of waiting ~4–5 half-lives
questions.why_correct: The loading-dose curve starts at the steady-state line from the first dose; maintenance-only needs ~4–5 half-lives (S26).

distractors.text: It permanently lowers the maintenance dose the patient will need
distractors.why: A loading dose does not change the maintenance dose itself (S26).

distractors.text: It eliminates the need for any therapeutic drug level monitoring
distractors.why: A loading dose does not remove the need for monitoring (S26).

distractors.text: It has no real advantage over maintenance dosing used alone
distractors.why: It reaches the target immediately (S26).

distractors.text: It shortens the drug's half-life so steady state comes sooner
distractors.why: Half-life is set by clearance and Vd, not by a loading dose (S19).

questions.stem: Approximately how many half-lives are required for a drug to reach steady state with regular, repeated dosing?
questions.correct: 4–5 half-lives
questions.why_correct: Steady state is reached in roughly 4–5 half-lives, regardless of dose size (S30).

distractors.text: 1–2 half-lives
distractors.why: Too few — steady state takes about 4–5 half-lives (S30).

distractors.text: 8–10 half-lives
distractors.why: Too many — steady state takes about 4–5 half-lives (S30).

distractors.text: After the first dose
distractors.why: That describes a LOADING dose reaching target (S26), not steady state from regular dosing.

distractors.text: 2–3 half-lives
distractors.why: Too few — about 4–5 half-lives are needed (S23, S30).

questions.stem: A patient with CKD is prescribed a renally-cleared, narrow-TI drug without dose adjustment. Which two consequences would you expect together?
questions.correct: Increased half-life and increased concentration
questions.why_correct: Reduced renal clearance raises both drug concentration and half-life (S48, S28).

distractors.text: Decreased half-life and decreased concentration
distractors.why: Lower clearance has the opposite effect (S28).

distractors.text: Increased clearance and decreased Vd
distractors.why: CKD DECREASES clearance (S15).

distractors.text: No change in either half-life or concentration
distractors.why: Reduced clearance raises concentration and prolongs half-life (S28).

distractors.text: Decreased half-life and increased concentration
distractors.why: Half-life is PROLONGED when clearance falls (S28).

questions.stem: A narrow-therapeutic-index medication requires monitoring. Which pharmacokinetic parameter most directly determines how long it takes to reach steady-state concentration?
questions.correct: Half-life of the drug
questions.why_correct: Time to steady state (about 4–5 half-lives) is governed by half-life (S48).

distractors.text: Bioavailability of the drug
distractors.why: Bioavailability is the fraction reaching circulation (Session 1), not the time to steady state (S48).

distractors.text: Route of administration
distractors.why: Time to steady state depends on half-life, not route (S48).

distractors.text: Chemical name of the drug
distractors.why: A chemical name describes structure; it has no effect on PK (S48).

distractors.text: Size of each dose given
distractors.why: Steady state takes ~4–5 half-lives regardless of dose size (S30).

questions.stem: A patient receives an IV dose that gives a starting plasma concentration of 100 mg/L. The drug's half-life is 6 hours. What is the plasma concentration at 18 hours?
questions.correct: 12.5 mg/L, with 87.5% of the drug eliminated
questions.why_correct: 18 h = 3 half-lives: C(t) = 100 × (1/2)^3 = 12.5 mg/L (87.5% eliminated) (S19).

distractors.text: 25 mg/L, with 75% of the drug eliminated
distractors.why: That is 12 h — 2 half-lives (S19).

distractors.text: 50 mg/L, with 50% of the drug eliminated
distractors.why: That is 6 h — 1 half-life (S19).

distractors.text: 6.25 mg/L, with 93.75% of the drug eliminated
distractors.why: That is 24 h — 4 half-lives (S19).

distractors.text: 3.125 mg/L, with about 97% eliminated
distractors.why: That is 30 h — 5 half-lives (S19).

questions.stem: Which statement correctly pairs each dose type with the parameter it is based on?
questions.correct: Loading dose is based on Vd; maintenance dose is based on clearance
questions.why_correct: Loading doses are based on Vd; maintenance doses are based on clearance (S23 notes).

distractors.text: Loading dose is based on clearance; maintenance dose is based on Vd
distractors.why: This reverses the pairing (S23 notes).

distractors.text: Both loading and maintenance doses are based on half-life alone
distractors.why: The lecture pairs loading with Vd and maintenance with clearance (S23 notes).

distractors.text: Loading dose is based on bioavailability; maintenance dose on Vd
distractors.why: Loading = Vd; maintenance = clearance (S23 notes).

distractors.text: Both loading and maintenance doses are based on clearance alone
distractors.why: Loading doses are based on Vd (S23 notes).

questions.stem: A drug is given every 8 hours instead of every 24 hours, keeping the same total daily dose. What happens to its average steady-state concentration?
questions.correct: It stays the same; only peaks and troughs change
questions.why_correct: The average steady-state level depends only on dosing rate and clearance; the interval changes only the swings (p. 51).

distractors.text: It triples because doses come more often
distractors.why: Total dose per day is unchanged, so the average is unchanged (p. 51).

distractors.text: It falls because each dose is smaller
distractors.why: Smaller, more frequent doses narrow the swings, not the average (p. 51).

distractors.text: It doubles because half-life gets longer
distractors.why: Dosing interval does not change half-life (p. 51).

distractors.text: It depends on Vd, which now changes
distractors.why: Vd sets the loading dose, not the average level (p. 51; p. 52).

deeper.why: Worked dosing math: steady state, loading and maintenance doses

definitions.text: **Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation changes an individual's response to a drug.**
Why the same dose does not work the same way in everyone.

**Allele:** one of the alternative forms of a gene at the same locus. **Haplotype:** a series of alleles inherited together on one chromosome. **Nonsynonymous SNP:** a single-base change that alters an amino acid.
**PM, IM, EM, UM:** poor, intermediate, extensive (normal) and ultrarapid metabolizer.

how.text: Genetic variation can alter drug metabolism (e.g., CYP enzyme activity).
It can alter drug transport across membranes.
It can alter drug target structure or expression.
It can alter overall drug response and risk of adverse reactions.
Personalized pharmacotherapy combines genotype, phenotype, disease state, and other medications into individualized therapy.
**Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation.**
Codeine is converted to morphine (200× more potent) by CYP2D6; CPIC recommends an alternative analgesic for CYP2D6 poor **and** ultrarapid metabolizers.
Clopidogrel: about 85% of a dose is inactivated by esterases; CYP2C19 activates the rest. CYP2C19 poor/intermediate metabolizers → prasugrel or ticagrelor.
TPMT intermediate activity: start thiopurines at 30–70% of the target dose; deficient: use a drastically reduced dose or an alternative.
Warfarin dose varies up to 20-fold between patients; CYP2C9 and VKORC1 genotypes explain much of it.

**G6PD deficiency** (X-linked, more than 400 million people): G6PD is the red cell’s only source of NADPH, so deficient cells hemolyze under oxidative stress such as infection, fava beans or certain drugs.
NUDT15 variants, as well as TPMT, cause thiopurine intolerance.

**OCT1 (organic cation transporter 1)** moves basic drugs such as morphine, tramadol, sumatriptan and ondansetron into the liver; people with two reduced-function alleles have about twofold higher levels.

clinical.text: CYP2D6 variation alters metabolism of many antidepressants and opioids (e.g., codeine activation).
CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing.
TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs (e.g., azathioprine).
Certain HLA alleles sharply raise the risk of severe hypersensitivity to specific drugs.
HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook pharmacogenomic screening consideration (seen again in the gout lecture).

examples.text: Codeine (CYP2D6), clopidogrel (CYP2C19), azathioprine (TPMT), allopurinol (HLA-B*5801); also antidepressants, opioids, PPIs.
CYP2D6 metabolizes up to one-quarter of clinically used drugs (β blockers, antidepressants, antipsychotics, opioids).
CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers: up to one-third of Ethiopians and Saudi Arabians; CYP2C19 poor metabolizers: 3–5% of Caucasians, 18–23% of Japanese.
**HLA-B*57:01** → abacavir hypersensitivity; **G6PD deficiency** → rasburicase contraindicated; slow NAT2 acetylators (~50% in the USA) → isoniazid toxicity.
**SLCO1B1 (OATP1B1)** reduced-function variants raise simvastatin exposure (221% higher AUC in homozygotes) and myopathy risk; CPIC advises a lower dose or another statin.
**ABCG2 (BCRP)** variant, common in East Asians (allele frequency about 30%), raises rosuvastatin levels; the label suggests half the dose.

traps.text: HLA-B*5801 before allopurinol = severe hypersensitivity risk — not absorption, not taste, and not irrelevant to drug selection.
Genotype is one input — never the sole basis for therapy.

hooks.text: Why can a CYP2D6 variant change codeine's effect? Codeine needs CYP2D6 activation — change the enzyme's activity and you change how much active drug is made.

high_yield.text: Pharmacogenomics = genetic variation changing drug response (metabolism, transport, target, ADR risk).

questions.stem: A patient is found to carry the HLA-B*5801 allele before starting allopurinol. Why does this matter clinically?
questions.correct: It flags a sharply higher risk of severe hypersensitivity
questions.why_correct: HLA-B*5801 is associated with severe hypersensitivity reactions to allopurinol — a textbook screening consideration (S36).

distractors.text: It predicts reduced absorption of allopurinol from the gut
distractors.why: The allele flags hypersensitivity risk, not absorption (S36).

distractors.text: It only affects how the drug tastes to the patient
distractors.why: It flags a severe hypersensitivity risk (S36).

distractors.text: It has no bearing on drug selection for this patient
distractors.why: It is a key pharmacogenomic screening consideration (S36).

distractors.text: It predicts faster CYP2D6 metabolism of allopurinol
distractors.why: HLA alleles relate to hypersensitivity; CYP2D6 relates to metabolism (S33).

questions.stem: A patient is about to start azathioprine. Testing shows TPMT deficiency. What is the main clinical concern?
questions.correct: Increased risk of toxicity from the thiopurine drug
questions.why_correct: TPMT deficiency raises toxicity risk with thiopurine drugs such as azathioprine (S33).

distractors.text: Reduced activation of the drug into its active form
distractors.why: Reduced activation is the CYP2C19–clopidogrel example (S33).

distractors.text: Severe HLA-associated hypersensitivity to the drug
distractors.why: That is the HLA allele example (e.g., HLA-B*5801 with allopurinol) (S33, S36).

distractors.text: Faster CYP2D6 metabolism of the drug and lost effect
distractors.why: CYP2D6 variation affects antidepressants and opioids (S33).

distractors.text: No concern, since genotype never affects therapy
distractors.why: Genotype is one input among several — it still matters (S34).

questions.stem: Which pairing of a genetic variant with the drug it most affects is correct?
questions.correct: CYP2C19 variation — clopidogrel activation
questions.why_correct: CYP2C19 variation affects clopidogrel activation and some antidepressant/PPI dosing (S33).

distractors.text: TPMT variation — codeine activation
distractors.why: Codeine activation is CYP2D6 (S33).

distractors.text: CYP2D6 variation — azathioprine toxicity
distractors.why: Azathioprine toxicity is TPMT deficiency (S33).

distractors.text: HLA-B*5801 — clopidogrel activation
distractors.why: HLA-B*5801 is tied to allopurinol hypersensitivity (S36).

distractors.text: CYP2C19 variation — allopurinol reactions
distractors.why: Allopurinol reactions are HLA-B*5801 (S36).

questions.stem: Which statement about using pharmacogenomic results best matches the lecture's personalized-pharmacotherapy model?
questions.correct: Genotype is one input alongside phenotype, disease, and other drugs
questions.why_correct: Pharmacogenomics is one input among several — genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation (S34).

distractors.text: Genotype alone should determine both the drug and its dose
distractors.why: Genotype alone never dictates therapy in isolation (S34).

distractors.text: Genotype matters only for drugs that are given by the IV route
distractors.why: Genetic variation alters metabolism, transport, targets, and response (S32).

distractors.text: Genotype affects adverse-reaction risk but never drug metabolism
distractors.why: Genetic variation can alter metabolism (e.g., CYP activity) (S32).

distractors.text: Genotype becomes irrelevant once a drug reaches steady state
distractors.why: Nothing in the materials limits genotype's relevance this way (S32, S34).

questions.stem: A 62-year-old has a coronary stent placed. Genotyping shows he is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. Which antiplatelet choice does CPIC guidance support?
questions.correct: Prasugrel or ticagrelor instead of clopidogrel
questions.why_correct: Clopidogrel needs CYP2C19 activation; poor metabolizers make little active drug, so prasugrel or ticagrelor is recommended (p. 81; p. 82).

distractors.text: Clopidogrel at the standard dose with routine follow-up
distractors.why: Standard clopidogrel risks stent thrombosis in poor metabolizers (p. 81).

distractors.text: Clopidogrel plus a CYP2C19 inhibitor to raise its level
distractors.why: Inhibiting CYP2C19 would reduce clopidogrel activation further (p. 81).

distractors.text: Codeine-free analgesia plus standard-dose clopidogrel
distractors.why: Codeine relates to CYP2D6, not antiplatelet choice (p. 81).

distractors.text: Azathioprine at 30–70% of the usual starting dose
distractors.why: That dose rule is for TPMT-intermediate thiopurine use (p. 83).

classes.name: Putting It All Together: Clinical Decision-Making

definitions.text: From concepts to clinical decisions: one integrated pharmacology pathway — Dose → Absorption → Distribution → Receptor / Target → Effect, with Metabolism and Excretion clearing the drug.
**Every topic in this lecture is a stop somewhere along this pathway — use it as your mental checklist when you evaluate any drug.**

how.text: Before you prescribe — the clinical decision-making checklist: Indication — is there a clear reason to treat?
Contraindications and allergies.
Renal and hepatic function.
Drug interactions (including CYP450).
Age, pregnancy, and other patient-specific factors.
Correct dose, route, and monitoring plan.
Memorize this list — it is exactly the checklist applied in the MSK cases (NSAID in CKD, methotrexate in pregnancy, etc.).

clinical.text: CYP interaction in action: a patient stable on a CYP3A4-substrate medication starts a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. **What happens to the first drug's level, and what would you watch for clinically?**
**Clinical pearl: always check for CYP450 interactions before adding a new drug to an existing regimen — one of the most preventable causes of toxicity.**

Agonist or antagonist? A new drug binds the same receptor as a home medication, and the home medication's effect weakens. **Is the new drug most likely a competitive antagonist, and how could you confirm it pharmacologically?**

**Clinical pearl: a competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — if raising the home medication's dose restores the effect, that supports competitive (rather than irreversible) antagonism.**

Study-guide case: 68-year-old woman, stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min), starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney; she started a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor 3 weeks ago.

Two concerns: reduced renal clearance from CKD will raise the antiarrhythmic's concentration and prolong its half-life regardless of the new drug; separately, if it has any hepatic/CYP3A4 component, the CYP3A4 inhibitor would compound accumulation further.

Before dispensing: check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and closely monitor renal function and signs of toxicity (arrhythmia worsening, other drug-specific toxicity) after starting.

If the drug were instead cleared by the liver via CYP3A4: the direct renal-clearance concern becomes less central (though CKD can still indirectly affect hepatic drug handling), and the CYP3A4 interaction becomes the dominant concern.

examples.text: Not covered in materials — the integrated vignettes use unnamed drugs ("a CYP3A4-substrate medication," "a home medication").

traps.text: The single check most aimed at preventing a toxic, predictable drug-drug interaction is reviewing CYP450 interactions — not brand name, chemical name, or half-life alone.
Weaker home-medication effect + restored by a higher dose = competitive; not restored = irreversible.
Reviewing indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and monitoring = the clinical decision-making framework — not pharmacogenomic testing or Phase IV surveillance.

comparisons.title: Key takeaways: the toolkit for every drug class
rows: Pharmacodynamics = what the drug does to the body (receptors, potency, efficacy).
Pharmacokinetics = what the body does to the drug (ADME).
Receptor interactions (agonism, antagonism) explain most drug effects.
ADME together determine how much drug reaches the target, and for how long.
Patient-specific factors — renal/hepatic function, genetics, interactions — determine the individual response.

hooks.text: Why check CYP450 before adding any drug? An inhibitor added to a stable regimen raises the other drug's level — predictable, so it is one of the most preventable causes of toxicity.
Checklist "**I C R I A D**": **I**ndication · **C**ontraindications/allergies · **R**enal/hepatic · **I**nteractions (CYP450) · **A**ge/pregnancy · **D**ose, route, monitoring.

high_yield.text: Memorize the checklist: indication, contraindications/allergies, renal/hepatic, interactions (CYP450), age/pregnancy, dose/route/monitoring.
**Always check CYP450 interactions before adding a new drug.**
These five ideas are the toolkit for every drug class for the rest of the course, starting with musculoskeletal pharmacology.

questions.stem: Before prescribing any new medication, which single check is most directly aimed at preventing a toxic, often-predictable drug-drug interaction?
questions.correct: Reviewing CYP450 interactions with the current medications
questions.why_correct: CYP450 interaction screening is one of the highest-yield steps for preventing predictable, preventable toxicity (S43).

distractors.text: Confirming the drug's brand name with the patient
distractors.why: Brand names don't screen for interactions (S43).

distractors.text: Checking the drug's chemical name in a reference
distractors.why: Chemical names describe structure; they don't screen interactions (S43).

distractors.text: Reviewing the drug's half-life alone before dosing
distractors.why: Half-life alone doesn't identify a drug-drug interaction (S43).

distractors.text: Confirming the route of administration on the order
distractors.why: Route is part of the checklist, but interaction review targets this risk (S39, S43).

questions.stem: A PA reviews indication, contraindications, renal/hepatic function, interactions, and a monitoring plan before prescribing. This process best reflects:
questions.correct: The clinical decision-making framework
questions.why_correct: This checklist is the clinical decision-making framework from "Putting It All Together" (S48, S39).

distractors.text: Pharmacogenomic screening of the patient
distractors.why: Pharmacogenomics is one input among several, not the whole checklist (S34).

distractors.text: Receptor pharmacology considered alone
distractors.why: Receptor pharmacology is one stop on the pathway (S38).

distractors.text: Phase IV postmarketing surveillance
distractors.why: Phase IV is postmarketing surveillance after approval (Session 1; S47).

distractors.text: Therapeutic index testing of the drug
distractors.why: TI compares toxic vs. effective dose; it is not this checklist (S47-48).

questions.stem: A drug has high potency but low efficacy compared with an alternative. For a patient needing maximum symptom relief, which factor matters more when choosing between the two?
questions.correct: Efficacy
questions.why_correct: Efficacy (the maximum achievable effect) matters more than potency for most clinical outcomes (S48).

distractors.text: Potency
distractors.why: Potency is the dose needed; it doesn't set the maximum effect (S48).

distractors.text: Both equally
distractors.why: Efficacy matters more than potency (S48).

distractors.text: Neither one
distractors.why: Efficacy predicts the maximum achievable benefit (S48).

distractors.text: Half-life
distractors.why: Half-life governs time to steady state, not maximal effect (S48).

questions.stem: Which best differentiates a competitive antagonist from a noncompetitive antagonist?
questions.correct: Noncompetitive lowers Emax; competitive shifts the curve right without changing Emax
questions.why_correct: Noncompetitive/irreversible antagonists lower Emax; competitive antagonists shift the curve right without changing Emax (S48).

distractors.text: Competitive lowers Emax; noncompetitive shifts the curve right with the same Emax
distractors.why: This reverses the two (S48).

distractors.text: They are pharmacologically identical and produce the same dose-response curve
distractors.why: Their curve effects differ (S48).

distractors.text: Only competitive antagonists cause adverse effects; noncompetitive ones never do
distractors.why: Adverse effects are not what separates them (S46, S48).

distractors.text: Competitive raises Emax; noncompetitive shifts the curve left at the same Emax
distractors.why: Neither raises Emax or shifts left (S48).

questions.stem: A patient starts a new drug that binds the same receptor as their home medication, and the home medication's effect becomes weaker. Raising the home medication's dose restores the full effect. What does this support?
questions.correct: The new drug is a competitive antagonist
questions.why_correct: A competitive antagonist can be overcome by increasing the agonist dose — restoring the effect supports competitive rather than irreversible antagonism (S41).

distractors.text: The new drug is an irreversible antagonist
distractors.why: Irreversible antagonism would NOT be overcome by raising the dose (S41).

distractors.text: The new drug is a strong CYP3A4 inducer
distractors.why: Nothing here involves CYP metabolism; it's receptor competition (S41).

distractors.text: The home medication has become toxic
distractors.why: A weaker effect restored by a higher dose points to competition (S41).

distractors.text: The new drug is a full agonist itself
distractors.why: A drug that weakens the home medication's effect is acting as an antagonist (S41).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old woman with stage 4 CKD (eGFR 24 mL/min) is starting a narrow-TI oral antiarrhythmic eliminated mainly unchanged by the kidney. Three weeks ago she began a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor. What is the best step before the prescription is filled?
questions.correct: Check eGFR/CrCl, lower the dose or extend the interval, and plan close monitoring
questions.why_correct: Reduced renal clearance will raise the drug's concentration and prolong its half-life; before dispensing, check eGFR/CrCl, consider a lower dose or extended interval, and monitor renal function and toxicity (SG U1-S).

distractors.text: Prescribe the standard dose, since only hepatic drugs are affected by CKD
distractors.why: CKD reduces renal clearance, raising concentration and half-life of renally-eliminated drugs (S15, SG U1-S).

distractors.text: Increase the dose, since the CYP3A4 inhibitor will lower the drug's level
distractors.why: A CYP3A4 inhibitor RAISES substrate levels (S6); induction lowers them.

distractors.text: Start the drug, and check renal function only if symptoms appear later
distractors.why: Check eGFR/CrCl and adjust BEFORE dispensing, then monitor closely (SG U1-S).

distractors.text: Shorten the dosing interval so steady state is reached more quickly
distractors.why: Intervals are EXTENDED in renal impairment; shortening raises accumulation (S17, S28).

summary.text: Metabolism inactivates drugs, activates prodrugs, or makes active or **toxic metabolites** (e.g., NAPQI); **Phase I** (CYP450 oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) functionalizes and **Phase II** conjugates for excretion.
A **CYP inhibitor raises** a substrate's level (toxicity) and an **inducer lowers** it (therapeutic failure) — always check CYP450 interactions before adding a drug.
The **kidney** is the main elimination route — filtration of free drug, active secretion, reabsorption of lipophilic un-ionized drug — and less renal function means less clearance and more exposure.
**Half-life** (time for concentration to fall 50%) depends on clearance and Vd: ~**4–5 half-lives** to steady state and ~**97%** eliminated after ~5.
**Loading doses** (based on Vd) reach the target immediately; **maintenance doses** (based on clearance) keep levels in range; in CKD adjust dose and/or interval by eGFR/CrCl.

**Pharmacogenomic** variants (CYP2D6, CYP2C19, TPMT, HLA-B*5801) change drug response, but genotype is one input in a checklist of indication, contraindications, organ function, interactions, patient factors, and dose/route/monitoring.
